newsitem.title: CHINA: China rules save schools, houses from bankruptcy.
newsitem.headline: China rules save schools, houses from bankruptcy.

text.p: China has passed new provisional regulations on bankruptcy of state-owned enterprises that forbid assets such as schools and housing from being used to pay off creditors, the China Securities newspaper said on Wednesday.
Under the new rules, state firms that declared bankruptcy would be able to sell off all types of liquid assets, fixed assets, invisible assets and outside investments, the newspaper said.
However, it said bankrupt enterprises could not use public facilities as secured properties.
"Workers' housing, schools and other public interest welfare facilities may not be handled as bankrupt properties and should be granted protection," it said.
Most Chinese state-owned enterprises were built in line with the self-sufficient commune theories of Chairman Mao Zedong and include schools, shops, hospitals and housing.
The rules say bankrupt enterprises, after paying legal fees for handling bankruptcy procedures, should give first priority to paying back the salaries and benefits of workers, it said.
The regulations allow for profitable portions of a bankrupt enterprise, such as a subsidiary or a production line, to be spun off with agreement from two-thirds of the creditors, it said.
Many of China's ailing state firms are technically bankrupt but Beijing has been reluctant to close them for fear that mass unemployment and loss of cradle-to-grave welfare could spark social unrest.

Official statistics show that more than half of China's state-run companies are losing money. But most have huge state bank loans outstanding and their bankruptcy would mean huge losses of state assets.
Beijing is also worried that a large unemployed population resulting from bankruptcies would lead to social instability.
With Beijing's blessing, local governments have actively promoted such takeovers, analysts said.
Analysts said takeovers in many cases helped listed firms enhance their efficiency and expand market share at a cheap price.

Shanghai Petrochemical pushed up its market share and increased its annual capacity of acrylic fibre output to 92,000 tonnes from 67,000 tonnes when it took over the Jinyang Acrylic Fibres Plant, one stock analyst said.
But analysts warned that some takeovers took place more because of administrative pressure than because they made economic sense.
And some listed firms appeared to have carried out takeovers in order to make their financial reports look better with revenues seemingly surging, they said.
